candidates.summary: The handler-level `_ran` count assertion is an upper bound with no floor and no payload check, so it passes over zero work whenever the handler returns early.
candidates.short_summary: _ran<=90 passes vacuously when no plan is active
candidates.failure_scenario: `get_training_plan_progress.handler` returns `_text({"active": False})` at tools.py:3765 whenever `plans.get_active_plan` is None. Measured in the worktree: with the perf fixture's plan row flipped to status='completed', `plans._ran` is called 0 times and the assertion `counts["n"] <= 90` passes green. Proof 2 in the plan is the one that says the fold actually reached the handler ('proof 1 alone can be satisfied by a folded helper nobody calls'), and it stops saying that the moment `_seed_plan` drifts, `get_active_plan`'s status filter changes, or the fixture's plan ages out. The sibling oracle test at :455 already carries the guard this one lacks (`assert payload.get("workouts")`), and this same diff writes an explicit anti-vacuity floor at :373 with the comment 'A query that quietly matched nothing must fail here, not pass over an empty loop' — so the change applies the rule to one of its three new count assertions and not to the other two.

candidates.summary: The `_round_floats` count assertion has the same vacuity hole — an early-return handler produces exactly one call, which is comfortably under the bound.
candidates.short_summary: _round_floats<=100 passes vacuously on an empty payload
candidates.failure_scenario: Measured in the worktree with no active plan: `_text({"active": False})` drives `tools._round_floats` exactly 1 time, and `assert counts["n"] <= 100` passes. Its own docstring calls it 'the assertion that binds the `_round_floats` change to a real reduction in work', which is exactly the claim that evaporates: a 1-call run and an 83-call run are indistinguishable to it. Anything that shrinks the fixture payload — a plan that stops seeding, `build_plan_detail` projecting fewer fields, a future compaction pass — silently converts this from a work-count proof into a tautology, and unlike a latency reading nothing else in CI would notice.

candidates.summary: The new docstring says the `bool` guard 'becomes load-bearing' under the int fast path, but the fast paths dispatch on exact `type()`, so the guard is still completely inert.
candidates.short_summary: docstring wrongly calls the bool guard load-bearing
candidates.failure_scenario: The plan predicted the guard would stop being dead code because the chosen implementation 'does' write an int fast path. It writes an exact-type one: `elif t is str or t is int or t is bool or v is None` (:198, :210). `type(True) is int` is False, so a bool never reaches the int arm — it is copied by the explicit `t is bool` arm — and the fallback ladder still has no int branch. Verified in the worktree by running the head implementation against a byte-identical copy with `if isinstance(obj, bool): return obj` deleted: 30,000 randomly generated payloads (dict/list/float/int subclasses, IntEnum, tuples, NaN/inf, -0.0, bytes, sets) plus targeted probes `True`, `False`, `{"x": True}`, `[True, False]`, `(True,)`, `{"aerobic_te": True}`, `[[True]]`, `{"a": [True]}` — zero divergences by both `repr` and `json.dumps`. The concrete cost is a reader (or a later refactor) trusting a stated invariant that no code and no test enforces: whoever next simplifies `_round_floats` will read this sentence, believe the guard is protected, and it is not. The plan's own rule — 'no test may claim removing it is observable' — is honoured; the docstring is what breaks it.
candidates.suggestion: below would make it load-bearing only if that path used ``isinstance``;

candidates.summary: The `_workout_actuals` equivalence oracle's '548 activity-days' corpus is 548 copies of a single shape, so its anti-vacuity floor counts days rather than distinct behaviour.
candidates.short_summary: 548-day oracle corpus is 548 copies of one case
candidates.failure_scenario: Measured against `build_perf_fixture_db` in the worktree: 548 dates, every one holding exactly 1 activity, all 548 typed `running`, and `avg_pace_sec_per_km` NULL on all 548 (scripts/perf_fixture.py:50-60 makes the paceless-ness deliberate). Every single day therefore returns `('running',)` via `_ran`'s label fallback — one branch, 548 times. The fold this oracle guards rewired three things the corpus never reaches: the walking branch, the `classes.add('other')`-then-`continue` for a non-foot row now sitting inside the accumulation loop, and any day holding more than one activity. `_WORKOUT_ACTUALS_EDGE_CASES` (:347) does not close it either — all six entries are single-element lists, so no case in this file mixes an on-foot and a non-foot activity in one day, which is precisely the interaction the fold moved. Concretely: a fold that dropped `classes.add('other')` on a mixed day would leave this test green over all 548 days and all 6 edge cases. (tests/test_plans.py:553 does cover the mixed day, so the repo is not blind — but the oracle sold in the diff and the plan as the guard for the fold is not the thing catching it, and `assert len(by_date) > 500` reads as if it were.)

candidates.summary: The adversarial case list covers a `dict` subclass (and mutates against it) but has no `list` subclass, leaving the symmetric `type(obj) is list` exclusion unguarded.
candidates.short_summary: no list-subclass case for the symmetric type() fast path
candidates.failure_scenario: The new code has two exact-type fast paths, `type(obj) is dict` (:192) and `type(obj) is list` (:204), and both deliberately shunt subclasses to the `isinstance` ladder. The corpus carries `_DictSubclass` (:419) and `test_the_round_floats_oracle_can_actually_fail` even builds a dedicated `_mishandles_a_dict_subclass` mutant for it — but nothing exercises a `list` subclass. A future edit that widened `type(obj) is list` to `isinstance(obj, list)`, or narrowed the ladder's `isinstance(obj, (list, tuple))`, would change how a list subclass round-trips and both proof 5 and proof 6 would stay green: proof 6 asserts only that *some* case diverges for each mutant, so the missing case is invisible there too. The same gap covers a tuple held as a dict value (`{"k": (1.2,)}`) — the dict fast path's `else` arm with a non-container child — which no case reaches either.

candidates.summary: `_WORKOUT_ACTUALS_EDGE_CASES` has no length floor, unlike its sibling `_ROUND_FLOATS_CASES`, so the only discriminating half of the fold oracle can be trimmed silently.
candidates.short_summary: edge-case list has no min-length floor
candidates.failure_scenario: `test_round_floats_output_is_identical_to_the_pre_inline_implementation` pins its corpus with `assert len(_ROUND_FLOATS_CASES) >= 20` (:458). `test_workout_actuals_still_answers_exactly_what_it_answered_before` pins the fixture side with `assert len(by_date) > 500` (:373) but nothing on the edge-case side — and per the finding above, the edge cases are the only part of that oracle that exercises anything other than a paceless labelled run. Deleting entries from the list (a merge resolution, a 'flaky case' removal) shrinks the discriminating corpus to zero while the test still reports a 548-day pass.

candidates.summary: The `dict` and `list` fast paths are 12 lines of near-identical copy-paste differing only in how the result is accumulated and where `dp` is resolved.
candidates.short_summary: dict and list fast paths are copy-paste twins
candidates.failure_scenario: Cost: the scalar-dispatch rule (`float` -> round, `str`/`int`/`bool`/`None` -> copy, anything else -> recurse) is now written twice, at :192-203 and :204-215, and any future change to it — a `decimal.Decimal` arm, a new high-precision key rule, a `bytes` case — has to be applied to both or the two containers silently disagree. The equivalence oracle would catch a divergence only if the corpus happens to hold that type in both a dict and a list position, which today it does not (see the list-subclass finding). The simpler form is one scalar helper the two loops share, e.g. `def _scalar(v, dp): return round(v, dp) if type(v) is float else v` plus a single `_SCALARS = (str, int, bool, type(None))` membership test, leaving each container branch as a three-line loop.

candidates.summary: `_count_calls` is a strict generalisation of the existing `_count_connect_opens`, and the diff adds it without collapsing the older one into it.
candidates.failure_scenario: Cost: two counting instruments in one file with identical bodies. `_count_connect_opens(monkeypatch)` (:83) is exactly `_count_calls(monkeypatch, db, "connect")`; the new helper's own docstring says so ('`_count_connect_opens`'s instrument pointed at a hot function'). The four existing connection tests could call the general one and the special-cased helper be deleted, so a later fix to the counter (thread-safety, resetting between calls, counting kwargs) does not have to be made twice or, worse, get made once and leave the two axes measuring subtly different things.

candidates.summary: The two mutants in the oracle-can-fail test are full 8-line re-implementations of `_round_floats_reference` rather than deltas from it.
candidates.short_summary: two mutants re-type the whole reference ladder
candidates.failure_scenario: Cost: the same five-branch ladder is now written three times in the file — `_round_floats_reference` (:333), `_ignores_high_precision_keys` (:474) and `_mishandles_a_dict_subclass` (:485) — with a one-line difference each. When the reference is refreshed (a new branch, a new high-precision rule), the two mutants have to be re-derived by hand or they stop being 'the reference minus one thing' and start being two unrelated functions that happen to diverge, which is not what the test claims to prove. A single `_mutant(kind)` closure, or passing the one differing behaviour in, keeps the delta visible and one-line.

candidates.summary: `_capture_progress_payload`'s wrapper is installed on the module attribute, so `captured.setdefault` runs on every recursive call, and the helper re-runs the whole handler once per test.
candidates.short_summary: capture wrapper fires on all 83 recursive calls
candidates.failure_scenario: Cost: the docstring says 'The first `_round_floats` call of the handler IS the whole payload', which is true — but because the real implementation recurses through the patched module global, `capturing` is entered 83 times per handler call and does a redundant `setdefault` 82 of them. It also means the helper is silently coupled to the recursion strategy it is measuring: if `_round_floats` ever stopped recursing through the module attribute, the capture would still work but the two work-count tests above would start reading 1. Two tests each pay a full `get_training_plan_progress` run for a payload that could be captured once by a module-scoped fixture and shared. Simpler: capture with an explicit `if "payload" not in captured` and hoist the whole thing to a fixture.
